Question: What are the things you hate to experience when selling your house?
Old_Answer: You can't help feeling emotional about the home you have lived in and loved. You've lavished thought and money over the decor. It's part of you in a way. So when potential buyers come round and wrinkle their noses at it, it's not nice. That's why estate agents are useful. They know what to say to get the sale. they don't care about the colour you painted the walls in, and if a viewer says something disparaging, they know not to defend the choice but to say how easy it would be to paint over it. Whenever I've sold houses in the past I've always gone through it thoroughly with the agent but then left it to them.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Selling a house can be a real trial by fire, and there are a few experiences that can really grind my gears. First off, the endless stream of viewings can feel like a never-ending parade of strangers traipsing through your home. You tidy up, make everything look perfect, and then someone comes in and leaves a trail of chaos behind them. It’s frustrating! Then there’s the dreaded lowball offers. After pouring your heart and soul into your home, it stings when potential buyers think they can snag a bargain. It’s like they don’t see the value in the memories and effort you’ve invested. And let’s not forget the waiting game. Once you’ve accepted an offer, the anticipation can be excruciating. You’re left hanging, wondering if everything will fall through at the last minute. It’s a rollercoaster of emotions, and not the fun kind. The paperwork is another headache; it’s like navigating a labyrinth of legal jargon that makes your head spin. You think you’re almost there, and then another document pops up that you need to sign. Finally, there’s the emotional toll. Leaving a place where you’ve built a life can be bittersweet, and it’s hard to say goodbye to the walls that have witnessed your journey. All in all, selling a house can be a real test of patience and resilience, and it’s not for the faint-hearted!

One of the things I absolutely detest is the unpredictability of the market. You’re constantly checking your phone for updates, hoping for a quick sale, but often finding yourself in limbo. All these factors combined can turn what should be an exciting new chapter into a stressful ordeal. Ultimately, while selling a house can lead to new opportunities, the hurdles along the way can be quite taxing, and it’s essential to be prepared for the emotional and logistical challenges that come with it.

Question: What changes in British society and culture have been most striking over the past 70 years?
Old_Answer: I'm almost 70. When I was a kid in London, everyone smoked. Really everyone, including doctors. It was slightly unusual if an adult didn't. Now the reverse is true. No one picked up after their dog. You had to watch where you were walking. Everything is cleaner now. In the past, car ownership was very aspirational. I remember, as a car-mad youngster, ruthlessly judging adults on the car they drove. No one cares much now. National Service was expected. When the Conservatives floated the idea of bringing it back at the last election…well, let's just say it wasn't a vote winner. Murderers were still being hanged. No one (apart from a few extremists) wants that again. In fact people nowadays are much more likely to show understanding and pity when someone commits a crime. Children were labelled "stupid" for having what we now know are a wide range of learning disabilities. People were very deferential. If you look at old interviews of Harold Wilson by Robin Day, they were almost grovelling compared to the more provocative techniques used now. Parents didn't challenge their children's teachers. Now it's commonplace. People went to church. Now most of the population is atheist. People were not very socially mobile in the past. You stayed in your lane. We move up and down much more now. In the past, casual racism and sexism was normal. Now it's very much frowned upon. I don't remember liking my parents' taste in music much, but my kids like mine. I can't say they play the Beatles for instance, but the see merit in them. Seventy years ago, Britain was determined to export manufactured goods at all cost. It was very keen on doing business with Europe and wanted to cooperate with our closest neighbours and markets as much as possible. Now, sadly, Britain is more isolationist. Britain was a real world power, with the remnants of an empire and huge clout in the world. That's changed dramatically. In the 1950's it wasn't very common to see someone with dark skin. Now Britain is home to a huge range of cultures that all feed in to a very diverse mix.

In the 1950s, women were largely expected to be homemakers, but today, they are prominent figures in every sector, from politics to business. The rise of feminism has not only empowered women but has also reshaped societal expectations around masculinity. Then there’s the multicultural tapestry that defines modern Britain. Post-war immigration has introduced a rich diversity of cultures, languages, and cuisines, particularly in urban areas like London, which has become a melting pot of global influences. This has, of course, sparked debates about identity and belonging, but it has also enriched the cultural landscape immeasurably. Additionally, the advent of technology and the internet has revolutionized communication and access to information, making the world feel smaller and more interconnected. Social media has given rise to new forms of activism and community engagement, allowing voices that were once marginalized to be heard. And let’s not forget the seismic shifts in attitudes towards issues like LGBTQ+ rights, which have seen a remarkable evolution from criminalization to celebration. While challenges remain, the progress is undeniable. All these changes reflect a society that is increasingly open, dynamic, and complex, moving away from the rigid structures of the past towards a more inclusive future.

Question: How can one negotiate with their landlord to lower the rent? What factors should be considered when determining the percentage of reduction to ask for? How can this amount be calculated?
Old_Answer: Offer the landlord something in return, such as maintaining and cleaning the common parts. If there is a green area, offer to keep it tidy and cut. Offer to clean the windows regularly. Offer a longer tenancy agreement to save the landlord costs of renewing the TA after a year. You have to understand that landlords are running a business. Anything you can offer to lower their costs will be of interest. Calculate the benefit to them by asking a professional company to quote on doing the work, then offer to do it for less.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Negotiating with a landlord to lower your rent can feel daunting, but it’s entirely possible with the right approach. First, gather data on comparable rental prices in your area; websites like Zillow or local listings can provide insight into what similar properties are charging. If you find that your rent is significantly higher than the market rate, that’s a solid foundation for your argument. Additionally, consider the current economic climate—if inflation is high or if there’s a downturn in the rental market, landlords may be more amenable to negotiation. When determining the percentage reduction to ask for, aim for a figure that feels reasonable; typically, a 10-20% reduction is a good starting point, depending on how far above market your rent is. Present your case clearly and respectfully, emphasizing your reliability as a tenant—if you’ve consistently paid on time and maintained the property well, highlight that. It’s also wise to consider the length of your lease; if you’re willing to sign a longer-term agreement in exchange for a lower rent, that could be a compelling incentive for your landlord. Lastly, be prepared for a counteroffer and remain flexible; negotiation is a two-way street. Ultimately, the key is to approach the conversation with a well-researched, calm demeanor, making it clear that you value your living situation but need to find a more sustainable financial arrangement.

First, it’s essential to gather data on the local rental market. Research comparable properties in your area to understand the going rates and identify if your current rent is above average. Factors to consider when determining the percentage of reduction to ask for include the length of your tenancy, your payment history, and any maintenance issues that have arisen during your stay. A common starting point for negotiation could be around 5-10%, but this can vary based on your findings. Be prepared to present your case clearly and respectfully, emphasizing your reliability as a tenant and any reasons that justify your request. Lastly, be open to negotiation; your landlord may counter with a different amount or offer other concessions, such as reduced fees or improvements to the property. Remember, the goal is to reach a mutually beneficial agreement that maintains a positive landlord-tenant relationship.

In time her position softened and she even owned an Audi Coupé, but it was her choice.

Question: Is it true that some doctors recommend smoking for health reasons? How much validity is there to this claim?

Answer_with_writing_sample: It's astonishing to think that there was a time when some doctors actually recommended smoking, often under the guise of it being beneficial for health. Back in the mid-20th century, tobacco companies cleverly manipulated public perception by enlisting physicians to endorse their products, claiming that smoking could alleviate stress or even aid digestion. This was a period marked by a shocking lack of understanding regarding the health risks associated with tobacco use. Fast forward to today, and the overwhelming consensus in the medical community is that smoking is detrimental to health, linked to a plethora of diseases including cancer, heart disease, and respiratory issues. The validity of any claim suggesting that smoking has health benefits is virtually non-existent in light of extensive research and evidence. While some may still cling to outdated notions or anecdotal experiences, the scientific data is irrefutable. It’s crucial to recognize that any perceived short-term benefits of smoking are vastly overshadowed by the long-term health consequences. The narrative has shifted dramatically, and now, rather than being seen as a remedy, smoking is rightly viewed as a public health crisis. So, if you hear someone touting the supposed health benefits of smoking, it’s essential to approach such claims with skepticism and a healthy dose of critical thinking. The medical community has moved on, and it’s high time the public does too.

Question: Do adult immigrants forget their native language after living in another country for years and raising children there?
Old_Answer: My Dad left Austria when he was 8 in 1938 and lived the rest of his life in London. He spoke perfect English without an accent and avoided speaking his native language. In fact I can only remember hearing him speaking German to a few aged aunts who couldn’t speak English. All the rest of the time the Austrian side of my family all spoke English together even when they were not with an English member of the family (like my mother) who spoke no German. However my father and I spoke German to each other on a few occasions. I can’t remember why. I learned my German in Frankfurt in the 1970’s and 80’s, and noticed his Austrian accent and rather quaint turn of phrase. He spoke it quite perfectly though.
Answer_with_writing_sample: It's a common misconception that adult immigrants completely forget their native language after years of living in a new country and raising children there. In reality, the situation is often more nuanced. While it's true that daily use of a new language can lead to a decline in fluency in the native tongue, especially if the immigrant is immersed in an environment where the new language is dominant, many retain a strong connection to their first language. This retention can be influenced by several factors, including the individual's motivation to maintain their native language, the presence of a community that speaks it, and the efforts made to pass it on to their children. For instance, I know several families where parents actively speak their native language at home, ensuring that their children grow up bilingual. This not only helps preserve the language but also enriches the children's cultural identity. However, if the immigrant becomes isolated from their native language community or stops using it regularly, they may experience a gradual loss of vocabulary and fluency. It’s not uncommon for them to struggle with complex conversations or find themselves searching for words. Ultimately, while some immigrants may lose proficiency over time, many retain enough of their native language to communicate effectively, especially in emotional or familial contexts. The key lies in the effort and environment surrounding language use, which can either foster retention or lead to gradual forgetfulness.

Ultimately, while some vocabulary and fluency may fade, the emotional and cultural ties to a native language often remain intact, serving as a vital link to one's identity and heritage. So, while it’s possible for adults to experience a decline in their native language skills, forgetting it entirely is less common, especially when there is a conscious effort to keep it alive.

Question: How can one cope with negative experiences while traveling abroad? Is the effort of traveling worth it if it is not enjoyable?
Old_Answer: We've all had disappointments. The theft. The horrible meal. The rude shop assistant. The delayed flight. Not all were actually disasters though, so let's not over-dramatise things. The way I deal with it is to learn from the incident but to travel more. So because I had a horrible experience skiing in France, I still ski, but I go to Austria. I have kind of done Milan where I was ripped off so simply don't need to go there again…etc, etc. I focus on what I like and what has been successful, and do more of that, and I try not to repeat mistakes. But I try to keep it in perspective…one rude Parisian isn't going to ruin France for me. Later this year I'm driving a 1967 Mustang Fastback from London to Vienna. My route is going to take in places I love in France, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland and Austria, places I've always wanted to see, and I'm sure there will be one or two incidents that don't work out too well. That will be all part of the adventure.
